Added in 4.13.0. `internal/opcuaserver` publishes this Gateway's configured
devices and tags as an OPC UA address space, so a third-party OPC UA client, a
SCADA package, an HMI, a historian, a test tool such as UaExpert, can read the
Gateway's live tags without anyone writing a HotLoop driver for the other side.
It is the server half of what `internal/driver`'s OPC UA client does in the
other direction, and it is the increment that makes "a third-party OPC UA
client reads Gateway tags" true.

Off by default (`HOTLOOP_OPCUA_SERVER_ENABLED`): opening a listener on a plant
network is something a deployment does on purpose. Default port 4840.

**It is read-only.** See [Why it is read-only](#why-it-is-read-only).

## What is exposed

One **Object** node per enabled device, directly under the standard *Objects*
folder, and one **Variable** node per enabled tag beneath its device. Devices
and tags that are switched off are not published, they have no worker and no
reading, so publishing them would only put a permanently Bad node in front of a
client. The address space is exactly what the runtime is polling.

Everything lives in one namespace, `urn:hotloop:ua:gateway`. The namespace URI
is a constant, not derived from the host name or the application URI: a client
stores a node as URI plus identifier and finds the namespace index again on
every connect, and a URI that changed with a pod name would orphan every
subscription a SCADA project has configured. Resolve the index from the
server's namespace array by URI, as a real client does; do not assume `ns=2`.

### NodeIds

Identifiers are strings, and stable:

| Node | NodeId identifier |
|---|---|
| Device | `<deviceId>` |
| Tag | `<deviceId>/<tagName>` |
| A tag's `EngineeringUnits` / `EURange` property | `~EngineeringUnits/<deviceId>/<tagName>` and `~EURange/…` |

The tag form is `model.TagKey.String()`, the `device/tag` spelling the rest of
the code base already uses, so a NodeId and a tag key convert into each other
with `model.ParseTagKey`. A `.` separator would not have worked: device ids may
contain dots, so `a.b.c` could be device `a` tag `b.c` or device `a.b` tag `c`.
A device id cannot contain a slash, so the first slash is always the boundary,
and a tag name that contains slashes (OPC UA browse paths and MQTT topics do)
still parses to the right device. Property ids start with `~`, which a device id
cannot, so a property can never collide with a tag whatever the tag is called.

### Attributes

| Attribute | Value |
|---|---|
| `BrowseName` | the device id / the tag name, in the HotLoop namespace |
| `DisplayName` | the device's name / the tag's name |
| `Description` | the device's or tag's description |
| `DataType` | see below |
| `ValueRank` | scalar (-1) |
| `AccessLevel`, `UserAccessLevel` | `CurrentRead` only (0x01) |
| `MinimumSamplingInterval` | the device's effective poll interval in ms, values cannot change faster than the runtime polls them, so a client asking for a faster sampling rate is revised up to it |
| `Historizing` | false |

A tag with a unit gets an `EngineeringUnits` property (`EUInformation`, unit id
-1 = "not a UNECE code", the unit text in `DisplayName`), and a tag with a range
gets an `EURange` property. A tag with neither has neither.

### Data types

The runtime reduces every numeric reading to a float64 in engineering units, so
the declared type is a presentation choice made in `kindForTag`, and it has to
be one the value can always be expressed in:

| Tag `dataType` | OPC UA type |
|---|---|
| `bool`, `boolean`, `bit`, `coil`, `discrete` | Boolean |
| `string`, `text`, `char` | String |
| `int16` | Int16 |
| `uint16`, `word` | UInt16 |
| `int32`, `dint` | Int32 |
| `uint32`, `dword` | UInt32 |
| `uint64` | UInt64 |
| `int`, `int64` | Int64 (the widest signed type, so nothing overflows) |
| anything else, including `float` | Double |
| **any integer type with a scale or an offset** | **Double** |

The last row matters: an `int16` register scaled by 0.1 reads 23.4, and
truncating it to an Int16 would hand a client 23 with a Good status. A value
that does not fit its declared type, an `int16` tag delivering 70000, is
reported `BadOutOfRange` with no value, never wrapped or clamped into something
that looks plausible. A numeric tag whose reading carries text is
`BadTypeMismatch`.

### Value, quality and timestamps

Each read (and each subscription sample) answers from the runtime's live cache, the same source `/api/values` serves, never from the database. The status
code is derived from that reading **and the state of the device link behind
it**, because the cache alone is not enough: it keeps the last reading a
device returned, and a device that has since dropped off the network still has
a perfectly good-looking last reading in it.

| Device link | Reading | Status | Value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Connected, at least one poll delivered this session | good | **Good** | sent |
| | uncertain | Uncertain | sent |
| | bad, or an unrecognised quality | Bad | none |
| Connected, no poll delivered yet this session | any | BadWaitingForInitialData | none |
| Connected, nothing cached at all | n/a | BadWaitingForInitialData | none |
| Degraded (session up, polls failing or partial) | good | **UncertainLastUsableValue** | sent |
| | uncertain | Uncertain | sent |
| | bad | Bad | none |
| Disconnected, connecting, disabled | any | **BadNoCommunication** | none |
| No worker for the device | any | BadOutOfService | none |
| Tag or device removed | n/a | BadNodeIdUnknown | none |

Good is only ever reported for a connected device, on a poll from the current
session, whose reading is good. A tag on a disconnected device reads Bad, not
its last value with a Good status.

Age is deliberately not part of this. Event-driven sources (an MQTT/Sparkplug
tag, an OPC UA subscription) legitimately hold a value for hours because
nothing changed, and calling it stale by the clock would be wrong; whether a
device is still delivering is the link's job.

**Source timestamp** is the reading's own timestamp, when the device was last
heard from, which is reported even on a Bad status. **Server timestamp** is when
the read was answered. Both are UTC.

## Subscriptions

Clients can create subscriptions and monitored items on tag variables and
receive data-change notifications, which is how SCADA clients actually consume
tags. Monitoring in this library is by sampling: the server reads each
monitored item on its sampling interval (at least 100 ms, and at least the
device's poll interval) through the same handler a Read uses, and notifies when
the value or the status changes. So a change in *quality*, a device dropping
off, is announced the same way as a change in value.

A monitored item on a tag that is removed is not left hanging: it receives
`BadNodeIdUnknown`.

## What a client sees while the configuration changes

When a tag is removed, reads of it and monitored items on it get
`BadNodeIdUnknown` straight away, and it drops out of a browse of its device
straight away. The node itself stays in the server's node table for about 5
seconds after that, unreachable, and is then deleted. A removed device works
the same way under the Objects folder.

An edit never leaves a gap. An edited tag or device is swapped for its new
version under the same NodeId in one step, so a read or browse at that moment
sees the old version or the new one, never "unknown". Subscriptions on it carry
on.

The delay before deleting is not decoration. The library's Browse reads a
node's reference list and then looks up each target without holding a lock
across the two, and if one target has vanished in between it fails the browse
of the *parent* with `BadNodeIdUnknown`, as if the device or the Objects folder
did not exist. We used to delete nodes outright, and a client browsing a device
while a tag was removed, or reading a tag while its device was edited, could
get told a perfectly real node did not exist. Do not go back to deleting nodes
directly in `space.go`: unlink first, delete later.
`TestAddressSpaceHasNoHolesWhileReconciling` catches it if you do.

## Why it is read-only

This increment does not implement writes, and says so in three places at once
so no single change can quietly add them:

- every published node has `AccessLevel = CurrentRead` and no write handler is
  installed, so a write is refused `BadNotWritable` and a client can see before
  it tries that the node is not writable;
- the roles the server hands out carry Browse and Read and nothing else, the
  library's default provider would make every logged-in user an *Operator*,
  which has Write, so this package supplies its own (`GetRoles`), and
  `TestRolePermissionsAreReadOnly` fails if a state-changing permission is ever
  granted;
- the tests write to a tag as a viewer, an operator and an admin, and assert the
  answer is `BadNotWritable` **and that the register on the device behind the
  tag did not change**.

The reason is that this project has one write gate, in `internal/runtime`:
`safety.allowWrites` (default off), the per-tag `writable` flag, range checks,
and an audit record with a reason for every attempt, including refusals. An
OPC UA write path would have to go through that gate, carry its principal into
the audit trail, and respect the master switch. That is a change with its own
review, not something to arrive as a by-product of publishing tags, and there
is deliberately no setting in this version that enables it.

## Security model

### Transport

Secure channels use the library's policies in Sign and SignAndEncrypt.
**`Basic256Sha256` is offered in both modes**, and this is what a client should
choose.

**SecurityPolicy None is an explicit opt-in**
(`HOTLOOP_OPCUA_SERVER_ALLOW_INSECURE`, default false), with a startup warning
when on. With it off, no None endpoint is advertised, and a client that opens a
None channel anyway can only run discovery: every other service is refused.
Even with it on, a user name and password still travels inside an encrypted
token (the token policy is `Basic256Sha256`, never None), though every value a
client then reads is unprotected.

**Known limitation: deprecated policies cannot be turned off.**
`github.com/awcullen/opcua` builds its endpoint list itself and offers, in
addition to `Basic256Sha256` and the `Aes128_Sha256_RsaOaep` and
`Aes256_Sha256_RsaPss` policies, the deprecated `Basic128Rsa15` and `Basic256`
in both modes. There is no option to remove them, and this package does not
fork the library to do so. A client only uses them if it chooses to; a network
policy cannot filter them out either, since the choice is made inside the
protocol. If your standards forbid them, this server does not meet them yet.

### Server certificate

If `HOTLOOP_OPCUA_SERVER_CERT_FILE` and `_KEY_FILE` are set, that RSA pair is
used as it stands. Otherwise a **self-signed application-instance certificate
is generated on first start and persisted** under `HOTLOOP_OPCUA_SERVER_PKI_DIR`
(`own/cert.pem`, `own/key.pem`, key mode 0600), so the next start presents the
same certificate and a client that was told to trust it once is not told again.
A warning is logged on every start while the certificate is self-signed, with
its SHA-1 thumbprint, the form OPC UA tools show, so an operator can compare
it with what a client displays.

The certificate says what OPC UA clients check, which an ordinary TLS
certificate does not: the **application URI** (`HOTLOOP_OPCUA_SERVER_APPLICATION_URI`,
default `urn:hotloop:gateway`, plus `:<siteId>` when one is configured) in the
URI subject alternative names, the host names and addresses clients use (the
endpoint host, `HOTLOOP_OPCUA_SERVER_CERT_HOSTS`, `localhost`, loopback, this
machine's host name) as DNS and IP SANs, and the key usages Part 6 lists for an
application instance. RSA-2048, five years.

A persisted certificate is replaced, with a warning that clients must trust the
new one, only if it can no longer do its job: less than 30 days left, an
application URI that no longer matches the configuration, a configured host it
does not cover, or a key that cannot be read.

**The machine's host name is not a configured host.** It goes into a new
certificate, but a persisted one is kept when the host name changes. In a
container the host name is the container's id, and in Kubernetes it is the pod's
name, so it changes on every redeploy. Until this was fixed it counted, and every
upgrade of a containerised Gateway minted a new certificate: Ignition, told to
trust the old one, refused the server with `Bad_SecurityChecksFailed` until
someone trusted it again, on every client, after every deploy. Clients reach the
server by `HOTLOOP_OPCUA_SERVER_ENDPOINT_HOST` and `_CERT_HOSTS`; set those, and
the certificate lives until it nears expiry. (A Gateway that has no endpoint host
set uses the machine's host name as the endpoint host, and that one does count,
since it is what clients are told. Another reason to set it.)

**A key can be unusable, and the server refuses it.** Upstream
[awcullen/opcua issue 57](https://github.com/awcullen/opcua/issues/57): when
the library decrypts a user-name token it sizes its ciphertext chunks from
`len(D.Bytes())` rather than from the RSA modulus size. `D` is a big integer,
so its encoding is one byte short whenever its top byte is zero, about **one
RSA key in twenty**, and every encrypted login against that key then fails,
every time, with the client seeing only "the secure channel has been closed".
Anonymous and unencrypted sessions are unaffected, which is what makes it easy
to misdiagnose. A generated key is drawn again until it is not one of these; an
operator-supplied key that is one is refused at start with an error that says
why. `TestUpstreamShortExponentBug` reproduces the failure against the library
directly, with no HotLoop code in between, and will start failing when upstream
fixes it, at which point the guard in `pki.go` can go.

### Client application certificates

OPC UA authenticates the application as well as the user. The server keeps a
trust list in `<PKI_DIR>/trusted/`: a client whose certificate is not there is
refused at the secure channel, and its certificate is written to
`<PKI_DIR>/rejected/`. **To approve a client, move its certificate from
`rejected/` to `trusted/`**, no restart needed; the directory is read on every
connection. `<PKI_DIR>/issuers/` and `<PKI_DIR>/crl` are passed through for
CA-issued client certificates; that path is the library's own and is not
exercised by this repository's tests.

`HOTLOOP_OPCUA_SERVER_TRUST_ALL_CLIENT_CERTS` (default false, with a startup
warning) skips this step. It removes application authentication only: a user
still has to authenticate with a HotLoop username and password.

### Who may log in

**User name and password, against HotLoop's own users.** There is one user
database, not a second credential store: the authenticator looks the user up
with the same `store.User` the HTTP login uses, compares with the same bcrypt
hashes (`auth.CheckPassword`), normalises the user name the same way (lower
case, trimmed), runs one bcrypt comparison whether or not the user exists so
that response time does not reveal which user names are real, and refuses a
disabled account. Unknown user, wrong password, disabled user and a user without
the permission all get the same answer, `BadUserAccessDenied`.

**A user may read tags only if their role grants `tags.read` and `values.read`**, the same pair the HTTP API guards `/api/tags` and `/api/values` with, resolved
through the same `auth.Permissions` and `auth.Allows`, so a built-in role and an
explicit permission list behave exactly as they do there. Both are required
because an OPC UA client browses the tag list and reads values through one
connection, and a user granted only one would otherwise get the other for free.
Every built-in role that has `values.read` also has `tags.read`; this bites only
for a user given an explicit permission list.

**Permissions are checked on use, not just at login.** The library asks for a
session's roles on every browse, read and subscription sample; those are answered
from a short-lived cache (10 s) of the user database. A user who is disabled,
deleted, or has permissions removed loses access on a live session within that
interval, with their monitored items turning Bad, rather than whenever their
client next reconnects. A lookup that fails counts as "no".

**Anonymous sessions are off** (`HOTLOOP_OPCUA_SERVER_ALLOW_ANONYMOUS`) and no
anonymous token is offered unless opted into, with a startup warning. X.509 user
identity tokens are out of scope and not offered. If HotLoop's own
authentication is off (`HOTLOOP_AUTH_INSECURE`) there are no users to log in as,
and the server refuses to start unless anonymous access is opted into.

A successful login is recorded in the system log the way an HTTP login is.
Failed logins are logged to the process log only, with the reason, so an
unauthenticated caller cannot fill the audit trail. At most four password
checks run at once, since each is a deliberately slow bcrypt comparison and OPC
UA has no equivalent of an HTTP rate limiter in front of it; beyond that there
is no lockout or rate limit, the same as the HTTP login.

The library keeps the decrypted user identity, password included, in the
session object for as long as the session lives. It is memory only and never
logged, but a heap dump of a running Gateway would contain the passwords of
the users currently connected.

**Limit: passwords longer than 64 bytes cannot log in over OPC UA.** HotLoop,
like bcrypt, accepts up to 72. A user with a 65-72 byte password can log in to
the web UI and not to this server (`BadIdentityTokenRejected`). Give an account
that needs OPC UA a password of 64 bytes or fewer.

I can't fix this from HotLoop's side, and here is why. The refusal happens
inside the library, before it asks HotLoop to check anything, so HotLoop never
sees the login and its log has no line for it. In `github.com/awcullen/opcua`
v1.4.0 (the latest release), `server/server_service_set.go` decrypts the
password, reads the length the client put in front of it, and rejects the
session when that length is under 32 or over 96 (lines 603, 663 and 723, one
per security policy). The length counts the password plus the 32-byte server
nonce, so the password tops out at 64 bytes. The endpoints and their token
policies are built inside the library too (`buildEndpointDescriptions` in
`server/server.go`) and there is no option to change either, so the only fix is
a change to the library: raise that 96 (nothing in RSA forces it, a 2048-bit
key carries more than that per block), or ship a fork. Searching that
repository's issues and pull requests for the password limit, `64 bytes` and
`plainLength` turns up nothing; its open #57 and #62 are about a different
decrypt bug (the buffer size when the key has a leading zero byte). No issue is
filed for this one yet. `TestAuthentication` pins the edge at 64 and 65 bytes so the
day a library upgrade moves it, the test fails and this paragraph gets
rewritten.

### Server diagnostics are removed

The library's per-session diagnostics nodes would let any logged-in user browse
every other session's user name and client address, so they are switched off,
and the `Server/ServerDiagnostics` object is removed from the address space
(its counters are also written without a lock by the library).

## Address-space changes at runtime

Devices and tags are added, edited and removed while the Gateway runs, and the
address space follows without a restart. **Mechanism: a runtime callback, plus a
timer as a safety net.**

- `runtime.Manager.OnReload` calls back after every successful `Reload`. Every
  device and tag mutation the API makes ends in a `Reload`, so a change made
  through the UI or API is published within moments. The callback only signals
  a reconcile goroutine; it never does the work itself, so a slow reconcile
  cannot stall the API request that triggered it.
- A periodic reconcile (`HOTLOOP_OPCUA_SERVER_RECONCILE_INTERVAL`, default 30 s)
  catches anything that changes configuration without a `Reload`.

Both run the same idempotent diff against the enabled devices and tags in the
database. It touches only what differs: an edited tag is replaced, a removed one
is deleted, and everything else, including the monitored items clients hold on
it, is left exactly as it was. The nodes of a new device go into the space in
one call, so a client browsing mid-reconcile sees a device with all of its tags
or none of it.

A callback was preferred to polling alone because the runtime already has the
one clean signal (`Reload`) and it makes a change visible in milliseconds
instead of up to a full interval; the timer stays because the address space
should not depend on every future writer of configuration remembering to reload.

## Connecting a client

The endpoint is `opc.tcp://<HOTLOOP_OPCUA_SERVER_ENDPOINT_HOST>:<port>`. In a
cluster the chart defaults the host to the release's Service DNS name; outside
one, set it to the name or address clients will actually use (a LoadBalancer
address, a DNS record), it is advertised in every endpoint URL and written into
the generated certificate. It is **not** where the server binds: the library
listens on every interface and takes only a port.

With UaExpert or any other client:

1. Add the server with that URL and choose `Basic256Sha256` / `Sign & Encrypt`.
2. Choose *Username*, and log in with a HotLoop user that has `tags.read` and
   `values.read`.
3. The first connection is refused because the server does not yet trust the
   client's certificate. Find it in `<PKI_DIR>/rejected/` (on the PKI volume in
   a cluster), move it to `trusted/`, and connect again.
4. The first time, the client asks whether to trust the server's certificate;
   compare the thumbprint with the one in the start-up log.
5. Browse *Objects* → the device → its tags, and drag tags into the data-access
   view; they subscribe.

## Ignition 8.3 as a client

**Verified on 2026-09-27 against Ignition 8.3.9**, the current stable release, in
Inductive Automation's own container image (`inductiveautomation/ignition:8.3.9`,
standard edition on its trial), against a HotLoop Gateway whose demo device
`extruder-1` is fed by a simulator. What was shown, end to end:

- an Ignition OPC UA connection to `opc.tcp://<gateway>:4840` with
  `Basic256Sha256` and `SignAndEncrypt`, signed in as a HotLoop **viewer**;
- the certificate trust in both directions, as below;
- OPC tags in Ignition's `[default]` provider pointing at HotLoop nodes, reading
  with Good quality and changing as the simulator moves. Every value Ignition
  showed was one HotLoop's own `/api/values` had held: the same double crosses
  the wire unchanged, so the lab compares them for equality, not closeness. A
  text tag declared `string` in HotLoop read "RUNNING" in an Ignition String tag;
- a write from Ignition refused: Ignition sent the write, HotLoop answered
  `Bad_NotWritable` (read off the wire over a Sign-only channel, where the
  response is signed but not encrypted), and HotLoop's value did not move;
- every security policy and mode Ignition offers, below.

`test/ignition/lab.py` does all of it again and prints PASS or FAIL for each
step; see its README.

Not verified: browsing HotLoop from the Designer's OPC browser (the Designer was
not used; the tags were created by item path, which is how the lab creates them),
Ignition's historian on these tags, and anything longer than the lab's runs.

### Setting it up

On the HotLoop side, before Ignition:

1. Turn the server on and set `HOTLOOP_OPCUA_SERVER_ENDPOINT_HOST` to the name
   Ignition reaches the Gateway by. That name is in every endpoint URL the server
   advertises and in its certificate.
2. Create a HotLoop user for Ignition with the **viewer** role (an admin does it
   with `POST /api/users`; see [AUTH.md](/iot/authentication/)). Any role with `tags.read` and
   `values.read` signs in; nothing more is offered, since the server is
   read-only.

In the Ignition Gateway (the web UI on port 8088):

3. On the **OPC Connections** page under Connections
   (`/app/connections/opc-client-connections`), create an **OPC UA** connection. Endpoint URL `opc.tcp://<gateway>:4840`;
   choose the `Basic256Sha256` / `SignAndEncrypt` endpoint; authentication
   **Username**, with the HotLoop user and password. The connection goes Faulted
   at once, which is expected: step 4.
4. **Approve Ignition in HotLoop.** Ignition's client certificate is now in the
   Gateway's `<PKI_DIR>/rejected/` (`/data/opcua-pki/rejected` in the container
   and the chart), named by its SHA-1 thumbprint, `<thumbprint>.crt`. Compare the
   thumbprint with Ignition's own OPC UA client certificate, shown on the OPC
   certificates page (`/app/connections/opc/security/certificates`). Then move
   the file to `trusted/`. No restart on either side.
   HotLoop does not log the refusal; the file is the only sign of it.
5. **Approve HotLoop in Ignition.** The connection now fails the other way: the
   status says `Bad_SecurityChecksFailed ... unable to find valid certification
   path`. HotLoop's certificate is in Ignition's rejected **client** certificates
   on the same page. Check its thumbprint against the one HotLoop logs at start
   (`generated a self-signed OPC UA application certificate ... thumbprint=`) and
   trust it. No restart; the connection comes up within seconds.
6. **Tags.** Create OPC tags with the connection as the OPC server and item paths
   in the namespace-URI form, which Ignition accepts as it stands:

   ```
   nsu=urn:hotloop:ua:gateway;s=extruder-1/Emberburn_Temperature
   ```

   Declare each one as what HotLoop publishes (see [Data types](#data-types)):
   Float8 for a float, Boolean, String, Int2 for an `int16`, Int4 for a `uint16`
   or `int32`, Int8 for the wider integers. They subscribe on the tag group's
   rate, and HotLoop revises a faster sampling rate up to the device's poll
   interval.

The same, as files or through the REST API (which is how the lab does it):

- The connection is the resource
  `data/config/resources/core/ignition/opc-connection/<name>/config.json`, profile
  type `com.inductiveautomation.OpcUaServerType`, or `POST
  /data/api/v1/resources/ignition/opc-connection`. Two things in it are not
  obvious. The password is an embedded secret, a JWE that `POST
  /data/api/v1/encryption/encrypt` makes from the plain text; a plain string is
  not accepted. And the `security` block needs the gateway's client key store
  alias and its password: leave it out and the connection fails with a
  NullPointerException, give an empty alias and it fails with `Unable to
  retrieve KeyPair for alias 'client'`. Copy the block from the stock
  `Ignition OPC UA Server` loopback connection, which carries both.
- The certificates are under `data/config/local/com.inductiveautomation.opcua/client/security/pki/`
  (`rejected/certs`, `trusted/certs`), or `GET
  /data/opc-ua/api/v1/client/pki/certificates/rejected` and `POST
  .../trusted/<sha1>` through the API. **Ignition does not name the files by the
  thumbprint**; the API's `signature` field is the SHA-1 thumbprint, and it
  matches what HotLoop logs.
- Tags go in with `POST /data/api/v1/tags/import?provider=default&type=json`.
- Every API call needs an API key (the API Keys page,
  `/app/platform/security/api-keys`), and a key only gets through if one of its
  security levels is in the gateway's read or write permissions (the
  `security-properties` resource). `test/ignition/lab.py` shows one way to set
  that up from files on a fresh gateway.

### What to expect

- **`Bad_SecurityChecksFailed` means two different things.** Ignition shows the
  same status when HotLoop refuses Ignition's certificate (step 4; the message
  has no reason) and when Ignition refuses HotLoop's (step 5; the message says
  *unable to find valid certification path*). Look in HotLoop's `rejected/`
  first.
- **A redeploy of HotLoop keeps its certificate.** Up to 4.15.3 it did not: the
  certificate had to cover the container's host name, which changes whenever the
  container is recreated, so every upgrade minted a new certificate and Ignition
  refused the server until someone trusted it again. That is how this was found,
  when the lab's HotLoop container was recreated mid-test. See
  [Server certificate](#server-certificate). The certificate still changes if the
  PKI volume is lost.
- **A text tag declared numeric reads `Bad_TypeMismatch`.** HotLoop publishes a
  tag as the type it is declared, and a `float` tag holding "RUNNING" cannot be a
  Double. Tags created by Discover tags up to 4.15.3 were all declared `float`;
  see [PROTOCOLS.md](/iot/protocols/#opc-ua). Declare them `string`.
- **Writes are refused, and Ignition blurs why.** HotLoop answers
  `Bad_NotWritable`. Ignition's own OPC UA server, asked to write the same tag,
  passes on only a generic `Bad` (0x80000000). The Ignition tag's value does not
  change.
- **The deprecated policies work, which is the point to note.** Ignition offers
  `Basic128Rsa15` and `Basic256`, HotLoop cannot turn them off (see
  [Transport](#transport)), and Ignition connects with them. Choose
  `Basic256Sha256` or one of the `Aes` policies in the connection.
- **The trial.** An unlicensed 8.3 gateway runs for two hours and then stops
  executing until the trial is reset in the Gateway web UI. Tags go stale when it
  lapses; that is Ignition, not the connection.

### Policy matrix

Each row is a fresh session with that policy and mode, reading live values:

| Policy | SignAndEncrypt | Sign |
|---|---|---|
| `Basic256Sha256` | works | works |
| `Aes128_Sha256_RsaOaep` | works | works |
| `Aes256_Sha256_RsaPss` | works | works |
| `Basic256` (deprecated) | works | works |
| `Basic128Rsa15` (deprecated) | works | works |

`None` is not offered unless `HOTLOOP_OPCUA_SERVER_ALLOW_INSECURE` is set, and
was not tried. `Aes256_Sha256_RsaPss` works here although it fails between
HotLoop's own driver and opc-plc: that failure is the driver's library, not this
server.

## Configuration

| Variable | Default | <span class="sr-only">Details</span> |
|---|---|---|
| `HOTLOOP_OPCUA_SERVER_ENABLED` | `false` | The feature is off until this is set |
| `HOTLOOP_OPCUA_SERVER_PORT` | `4840` | TCP port, on every interface |
| `HOTLOOP_OPCUA_SERVER_ENDPOINT_HOST` | this machine's host name | What clients are told to connect to; also written into a generated certificate. **Set this.** |
| `HOTLOOP_OPCUA_SERVER_APPLICATION_URI` | `urn:hotloop:gateway[:<siteId>]` | Must stay stable across restarts; must be a URI |
| `HOTLOOP_OPCUA_SERVER_PKI_DIR` | `/data/opcua-pki` | Certificate, key, `trusted/`, `rejected/`. Back it with a volume |
| `HOTLOOP_OPCUA_SERVER_CERT_FILE` / `_KEY_FILE` | n/a | Use this RSA pair instead of generating one; set both or neither |
| `HOTLOOP_OPCUA_SERVER_CERT_HOSTS` | n/a | Extra DNS names / IPs for a generated certificate |
| `HOTLOOP_OPCUA_SERVER_ALLOW_INSECURE` | `false` | Offer SecurityPolicy None. Warned about at startup |
| `HOTLOOP_OPCUA_SERVER_ALLOW_ANONYMOUS` | `false` | Accept sessions with no identity. Warned about at startup |
| `HOTLOOP_OPCUA_SERVER_TRUST_ALL_CLIENT_CERTS` | `false` | Skip client-certificate approval. Warned about at startup |
| `HOTLOOP_OPCUA_SERVER_MAX_SESSIONS` | `20` | 0 = unlimited |
| `HOTLOOP_OPCUA_SERVER_MAX_SUBSCRIPTIONS` | `200` | 0 = unlimited |
| `HOTLOOP_OPCUA_SERVER_RECONCILE_INTERVAL` | `30s` | The safety-net reconcile period |

The server is not started in `--mcp-stdio` mode: that is an agent spawning this
binary as a helper, and a second process contending with the real Gateway for
port 4840 is not something that should be possible.

### Helm

`opcuaServer.*` in `charts/hotloop/values.yaml`. Enabling it adds a Service
(`<release>-opcua`, ClusterIP by default, LoadBalancer or NodePort is a
deliberate choice for a client outside the cluster), a PVC for the PKI
directory (`opcuaServer.persistence`; losing it means every client must trust
a new certificate), the container port, and, so that `networkPolicy.enabled`
and `opcuaServer.enabled` together do not silently leave a server listening
that nothing can reach, the port in the default NetworkPolicy ingress rule.
A custom `networkPolicy.ingress` replaces that rule, as it does for the broker,
and must then list the port itself. `opcuaServer.tls.existingSecret` supplies a
`kubernetes.io/tls` Secret instead of a generated certificate.

## Dependency

`github.com/awcullen/opcua` v1.4.0 (MIT), the only Go OPC UA library found that
ships a real server package. Choices worth knowing:

- **v1.4.0, the latest tag (December 2024), not master.** Master has newer
  commits (through February 2026), but the difference is a `DeleteNode` API
  refactor, not fixes for anything here; a pinned release is what this
  repository does everywhere else.
- **Six modules join the build**: the library itself, `djherbis/buffer` (MIT),
  `gammazero/deque` (MIT), `gammazero/workerpool` (MIT), `google/uuid` (BSD-3)
  and `pkg/errors` (BSD-2). The ~39 figure in the search results is the whole
  module graph including test-only dependencies; none of those are compiled in.
  All licences are permissive, none is vendored or modified, so `NOTICE`, which lists only vendored or modified code and non-permissive licences, is
  unchanged.
- **No cgo.** The binary still builds with `CGO_ENABLED=0` and runs on
  `distroless/static`.
- **Binary size**: `linux/amd64`, `-trimpath -ldflags="-s -w"`, went from
  23,634,082 to 28,598,434 bytes (+4.7 MiB, +21%). About 2.9 MB of that is the
  library's embedded OPC UA nodeset XML.
- **Two OPC UA libraries in one binary.** `internal/driver` uses
  `github.com/gopcua/opcua` for the client; the server uses `awcullen/opcua`.
  They share no packages or global state; it builds and runs. The client was not
  migrated.

### What was found in the library

Beyond issue 57 above (worked around) and the deprecated policies (documented):

- **A data race in `Server.Close`**, found by the race detector, not by
  reading. `Close` writes the shutdown reason and the seconds-till-shutdown
  countdown without a lock while the `ServerStatus` read handlers read them from
  the sampling goroutines, so any client that monitors `ServerStatus`, most
  SCADA clients do, races the server's own shutdown. This package answers those
  three nodes itself, from state it guards, and reproduces the countdown
  (`status.go`); `TestShutdownWhileServerStatusIsMonitored` fails under `-race`
  without that.
- **`Server.Close` panics if called twice** (it closes a channel
  unconditionally) and **sleeps three seconds first**, so `Stop` takes a few
  seconds. Stop is guarded to close once.
- **`ListenAndServe` binds `:<port>` on every interface** and has no
  bind-address option; a failed listen leaves the server's background
  goroutines running (upstream issue 43), which `Start` cleans up by closing it.
- **A discovery-only channel dereferences `DiscoveryURLs[0]`**, which panics on
  the first unauthenticated connection if the application description has none;
  it is always set here.
- **Unsynchronised diagnostic counters** (from reading the code; not
  reproduced): the library increments its `serverDiagnosticsSummary` counters
  from every connection's goroutine without synchronisation whenever a login is
  refused, so two clients refused at the same instant would race. Only counters
  could be corrupted, and nothing here reads them (the subtree is removed), but
  the writes themselves are upstream's and remain.
- **One polling goroutine and ticker per distinct sampling interval**, never
  reclaimed until the server closes; a client using many distinct intervals grows
  them, bounded by the interval range (100 ms to 60 s).
- **Empty token policy id** (fixed in 4.15.0): the library requires a client to
  echo the token policy id from the endpoint list, as the specification says.
  This repository's own OPC UA *driver* used to build its client with
  `AuthAnonymous()` and `AuthUsername()` and no endpoint selection, so it sent an
  empty policy id and could not open a session against this server in any mode
  (`BadIdentityTokenInvalid`). That was a fault in the driver, found by trying it
  against this server. The driver now asks the server for its endpoints, picks the
  one that matches the device, and echoes the policy id it listed, so this
  Gateway can be a device of another Gateway: a user name and password over
  `SignAndEncrypt` works, the driver's certificate is approved by moving it from
  `rejected/` to `trusted/` here, and this server's certificate is approved on the
  driver's side the same way. The refusal of a client that still omits the id is
  kept as a test, as the control that shows the server was right. See
  [PROTOCOLS.md](/iot/protocols/#opc-ua-security-and-credentials).

## What has and has not been verified

**Tested**, not **verified**, this repository's own distinction between the
two. Every test client is [`github.com/gopcua/opcua`](https://github.com/gopcua/opcua),
a genuinely independent implementation: the server is `awcullen/opcua` and the
two share no code, so a passing test means two implementations agree on the
wire. Everything behind the server is real, a real Modbus server holding real
registers, the real driver, runtime and cache polling it, a real
TimescaleDB holding real users with real bcrypt hashes, and nothing is mocked.

Tested, with a `gopcua` client over `Basic256Sha256` / `SignAndEncrypt` and a
user name and password:

- browsing the address space (device objects, tag variables, properties);
- reading a tag and asserting value, declared data type, status, source and
  server timestamps, for every mapped type;
- creating a subscription and receiving data-change notifications when the
  underlying register changes, when a device is unplugged (the tag turns Bad)
  and when it returns;
- a tag on a disconnected device reading Bad even though a Good reading is in
  the cache, and a partly failing device reading no better than Uncertain;
- the address space following devices and tags being added, edited, removed and
  switched off, by reload and by the periodic reconcile, including a monitored
  item on a removed tag turning `BadNodeIdUnknown`;
- start, stop, restart and stop-while-connected, with the certificate surviving
  restarts, a port already in use, and a client monitoring `ServerStatus`
  during shutdown;
- the negative paths, each of which fails for the reason under test (the error
  carries the specific OPC UA status) and each of which has a matching
  acceptance from the same client code: a wrong password, an unknown user, a
  disabled user, a user whose role lacks `tags.read` or `values.read`, anonymous
  with anonymous access off, SecurityPolicy None with insecure mode off, a
  client certificate that is not trusted (and its approval), a write to a tag
  as viewer, operator and admin, and permission revoked on a live session;
- the whole suite under `go test -race -count=10`.

**Verified against Ignition 8.3.9**, a production SCADA client built on a third
OPC UA stack (Eclipse Milo): reads, subscriptions, a refused write, and every
security policy it offers, including the `Aes*` and the deprecated ones. See
[Ignition 8.3 as a client](#ignition-83-as-a-client).

**Not verified** against UaExpert, KEPServerEX, WinCC, or any OPC
Foundation-certified client or the OPC UA compliance test tool. Also not
verified: CA-issued client certificates and CRLs; behavior with thousands of tags or hundreds of
subscriptions; IPv6; and any client that expects features this server does not
implement (history, events, methods, writes, X.509 user tokens).
